title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 84
paragraphs: Meanwhile, to Croesus himself it happened thus. He had a son, of whom I made mention before, who was of good disposition enough but deprived of speech. In his former time of prosperity Croesus had done everything that was possible for him, and among the other things which he devised, he had sent messengers to Delphi to inquire concerning him. The Pythian prophetess spoke to him thus:

“Lydian, master of many, much blind to destiny, Croesus, do not desire to hear in your halls that voice which is prayed for—the voice of your son. Much better if this were removed from you, since he shall first utter speech on an evil day of misfortune.”

Now when the fortress was being taken, one of the Persians was about to slay Croesus, taking him for someone else. Croesus, for his part, seeing the man coming on, cared nothing for it because of the misfortune which was upon him, and to him it was a matter of indifference that he should be slain by the blow. But this voiceless son, when he saw the Persian coming on, through terror and anguish burst the bonds of his utterance and cried out: “Man, do not kill Croesus.” This son, I say, spoke then for the first time of all, but after this he continued to use speech for the whole rest of his life.
